Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Environment and Natural Resources; l am Anya Trundy, a Deputy Commissioner for the Department of Administrative and Financial Service (DAFS) and I am here today to provide
testimony in Opposition to this bill on behalf of the Bureau of General Sen/ices (BGS).
I want to start by recognizing that many Committee members may be unaware of how the State came to own the Juniper Ridge Landfill. JRL was previously the West Old Town landfill associated with the Georgia-Pacific owned mill located in Old Town. ln 2004, the State of Maine
purchased the landfill from G-P for $26 million cash provided by Casella under the OSA. This took the long-term liability of the landfill off the mill's balance sheet, as well as, provided much needed capital for G-P to build a biomass plant to reduce the mill's energy expenses, with the larger objectives of keeping the mill in operation, saving the jobs of those employed at the mill, and presenling a substantial percentage of Old Town's property tax base.
Opposition to the landfill has existed since the Legislature approved the original purchase.
Nobody wants a landfill in their backyard, but whether you support or oppose JRL we all
contribute to the generation of waste that needs to be disposed of. In 2003, the acquisition of
JRL provided a desperately needed location for municipal waste and Casella was contracted to operate the landfill in a manner revenue-neutral to the State. Today, expansion of JRL is critical
to maintaining the state's solid waste disposal capacity, providing the necessary disposal of bypass municipal solid waste for communities effected by the shutdowns of other processing facilities and disposal of sludge from municipal wastewater districts.
DAFS has not exceeded the authority granted to us by the Legislature when the State assumed ownership of JRL. Contrary to misinformation recently circulating among legislators; I want to be
clear that BGS, has I191 extended the current and original 30-year Operating Services Agreement

In Opposition to L.D. 1349, An Act to Require Legislative Approval for a Contract to

April 28, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Environment and Natural Resource, my name is Ashley Luszczki. I am here on behalf of the Maine
State Chamber of Commerce, representing a network of 5,000+ small to large businesses. Thank you
for the opportunity to provide testimony in opposition to L.D. 1349, An Act to Require Legislative
Approval for a Contract to Operate the Juniper Ridge Landfill.
Our mission is to promote a positive business climate and advance policies that foster long-term economic growth in Maine. Proposals like L.D. 1349 inject risk into our business climate by adding a new layer of uncertainty to the regulatory process. This kind of unpredictability is precisely what deters businesses from investing or partnering with the state on critical infrastructure needs. Regardless of the issue, the Maine State Chamber of Commerce would strongly oppose contract approvals by the
Legislature.
The process for awarding a contract to operate the state-owned Juniper Ridge Landfill is and should remain a function of the appropriate executive branch agencies, specifically the Department of Administrative and Financial Services (DAFS), in coordination with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). These agencies have technical expertise, regulatory responsibility, and public accountability to ensure that contracts align with Maine's environmental standards, operational needs, and long-tenn waste management goals.
Again, the Chamber believes that subjecting contracts -- whether for approval or renewal - to legislative approval risks politicizing what should be a data-driven, regulatory decision-making
process. We believe it would set a precedent where routine procurement agreements could be delayed
or affected by other legislative debates. This creates uncertainty for businesses, undermines the . integrity of the procurement process, and could ultimately drive away experienced, qualified operators.
State-owned assets must be managed with public interest at the forefront, and we believe the current,
multi-step process provides appropriate oversight and public engagement. L.D. 1349 would signal to current and prospective business partners that the State of Maine is an unpredictable place to do business. At a time when Maine is working hard to attract private investment and modernize its infrastructure, this bill could negatively impact partnerships and procurements.

10046804:
April 27, 2025
RE LD1349: An Act to Require Legislative Approval for a Contract to Operate the Juniper Ridge Landfill
Dear Committee Members,
I am writing to express my strong support for LD1249, a bill which would require Legislative approval before entering into or renewing a contract to operate the Juniper Ridge Landfill. I am a resident of Old Town, one of several communities which are most directly impacted by what happens at Juniper Ridge.
Juniper Ridge is a major, state owned facility which accepts waste from all over Maine, and at times has also accepted waste from outside Maine. However, while the state as a whole may benefit from having a place to dispose of its waste, the local community, including both Old Town and our immediate neighbors, the Penobscot Nation, bear the brunt of the odor, traffic, and toxic smoke that occur intermittently from fires at the landfill. These issues impact the health and safety of our communities, as well as sensitive wetland areas in the Penobscot river basinyet we have no say in the regulation or mitigation of pollution coming from the landfill, pollution which makes fish unsafe to eat and water unsafe to drink for humans, birds, and other living things. These hazards will be made significantly worse by the major expansion currently being proposed for Juniper Ridge.
Currently, decisions are made about landfill expansion through an administrative process which only pays lip service to public concerns. For example, at several "public information sessions," Juniper Ridge contractors insulted members of the public by assuring us that the landfill would not add to the burden of PFAS and other contaminants impacting environmental quality in our region; despite that fact that community members already experience toxic smoke and unsafe water. Additionally, the extent of the pollution caused by the landfill at its current size has never been adequately evaluated and, with regards to the fires that sometimes erupt from the landfill, have been actively denied by the landfill operator, Cassella Waste Management.
The contractors who spoke at these community "informational" events were employed by Cassella to present their position in glossy powerpoints, just as they do to state administrators who currently hold decision making power over contracting with Cassella. These contractors were either ill equipped or unwilling to answer many hard questions from local residents. Yet DEP determined that these educational sessions had fulfilled the requirement for informing the community finding no violation of the "environmental justice" requirement of the review process. Given the strong objection of many Old Town community members and the Penobscot Nation to expanding Juniper Ridge, and the lack of representation we collectively suffered in the determination process, this finding would be laughable if it wasn't ultimately dangerous.
In contrast to the current inequitable process, LD 1349 will, if enacted, ensure that decisions about this state-owned landfill would be made by the Maine Legislature, a body which is elected by and accountable to the people of the state to protect the public good. Because there are many public and environmental health concerns from the current landfill operations which are not being addressed, this bill would provide the Legislature opportunity to investigate and address critical issues prior to any contracting.

Additionally LD1349 will facilitate a transparent conversation about how much waste should be brought to Juniper Ridge from other parts of Maine, how much risk the rest of the state is asking our local communities to absorb, and whether any of this meets Maine's environmental goals, including its commitment to environmental justice. I have confidence that elected officials, who are accountable to their constituents wherever they may be in Maine, will understand the need to meaningfully include community concerns in decision making processes.
Old Town, the Penobscot Nation, surrounding communities, and the Penobscot River have born the brunt of air and water contamination caused by Juniper Ridge Landfill even at its current size. However, the administrative review process in existence now has entirely ignored our concerns and prioritized corporate profit over community health. We do not consent to being a sacrifice zone and deserve a decision- making process which includes the voice of those who would be most directly impacted by the proposed landfill expansion.
I urge the Committee to vote in favor of LD1349, to ensure fair representation and accountability for decisions made about waste management in Maine and specifically for Juniper Ridge Landfill.
Sincere regards,
Daisy Goodman
Old Town, ME

LD 1349 Testimony in Favor
Senator Tepler, Rep. Doudera, and Members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee,
This history of the Juniper Ridge Landfill (JRL), Maine's only functioning state landfill, is replete with examples of bad government. Born in a "Mill Crisis" its Operator was chosen before sending out a Request for Proposals (RFP). The chosen Operator, Casella Waste Systems, refused to honor the $50 million bond requirement in the RFP after being awarded the contract. State and waste company officials proclaimed that "There will be no out of state waste allowed" at the same time they had signed an agreement facilitating importation.
In 2006 another "Mill Crisis" led to the 2nd amendments to the Operating Services Agreement, and the Fuel Supply Agreement opened up Maine's state landfill to almost unlimited imports of out of state Construction and Demolition Debris (CDD). We call these OSA amendments the Secret Amendments because the participants neglected to inform the local municipalities or their elected officials. The DEP, as Regulator of JRL, was left out of the loop! Our JRL Advisory Committee was not advised of these major changes and the Public was excluded until some of us finally realized that there was a change, but it took us until 2008 to understand what had happened.
LD 1349 would restore the power of the legislature to determine the future operation of JRL or any other state landfills. Currently the only guiding principle is for Casella to make as much profit as possible. This includes actions that put the Public Health at risk. Currently Casella has uncovered acres of JRL and is putting more waste in place where the landfill has settled. This unleashes landfill gases, notably methane (a powerful greenhouse gas) into our atmosphere, and the stench of partially decayed garbage spreads over the area for miles around. The public suffers, Casella profits, the State does little to control its own landfill!
Is there any other contract between the State agencies and corporations that come close to the amount of money involved at JRL? There have already been 20 million cubic yards permitted and almost filled. Each one of these cubic yards has to be worth at least $50 to $100, which means there has been at least a billion dollars of landfill capacity awarded. This should not continue without enhanced oversight and approval by our State Legislature, which holds the Public trust for Maine property.
The Bureau of General Services (BGS) is the titular owner of JRL. Early last year they held a Public Hearing on whether or not to Extend the JRL OSA beyond its 2034 end date. The Pubilc spoke unanimously against extension. BGS received voluminous comments, but never answered to specific questions and allegations raised by we participants. The State as Owner has always given Casella whatever they wanted, and

that has hurt the Citizens of this area, including the Penobscot Indian Nation. LD 1349 will reassert control of Maine's waste problems by mandating legislative involvement and approval of ongoing contracts. I urge you to vote Ought to Pass.
Respectfully yours,
Ed Spencer

Testimony to the Committee on Environment and Natural Resources April 28, 2025
Re: Support for LD 1349: An Act to Require Legislative Approval for a Contract to Operate the Juniper Ridge Landfill
Juniper Ridge is Maine's only active, state-owned landfill. As such, it is the concern of all Mainers, and any contract for its operation must be made with the full participation of the Maine Legislature.
The need for this legislation derives from several factors:
1. Juniper Ridge must align with Maine's environmental goals and solid waste hierarchy.
2. The landfill was intended for Maine's solid waste, but it is accepting an increasing amount of out-of-state waste.
3. It has been the source of ongoing problems, such as fires, odors, noise, and traffic. For many years, residents of Old Town and members of the Penobscot Nation have expressed concern about these issues, generally with little recourse or response. These serious public health and safety matters warrant greater scrutiny.
4. The landfill is situated near ecologically sensitive areas and Penobscot Nation lands, and its leachate has long poisoned the Penobscot River with PFAS and other toxins.
5. Residents of towns beyond the immediate area are affected when their municipalities transfer waste to the landfill, for which they pay tipping fees, and of course by the downstream effects of PFAS pollution.
Contracts for the state-owned landfill's operation are long-term and not to be taken lightly. No further contracts, or contract renewals, should be awarded without legislative approval. The involvement of our elected officials, who are accountable to the people of Maine, prioritizes the public good over private gain. Ensuring legislative approval for future landfill contracts provides for an open, visible process to evaluate landfill operations. I urge you to support LD 1349.
Thank you for the opportunity to express my opinion.

Good morning Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee:
My name is Nora Bosworth, and I am a Staff Attorney with the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF). CLF's mission is to conserve natural resources, protect public health, and build healthy communities in Maine and throughout New England.
CLF enthusiastically supports LD 1349, which would require legislative approval for any contract or contract renewal for the operation of the state-owned Juniper Ridge Landfill (JRL).
The Operating Services Agreement ("the contract") for JRL is between the Bureau of General Services (BGS) and Casella. The bill should be amended to reflect this, but the motivation and spirit of the bill are absolutely correct. For years, the public has watched Casella attempt to strong-arm the State to benefit Casella's profits at Mainers' expense. LD 1349 would give the public greater input into the terms governing this state-owned landfill.
In 2022, Mainers pushed to close a legal loophole that allowed Casella to fill up about one-third of JRL with construction waste from Massachusetts. Casella vehemently opposed the reform, claiming that it would force the closure of the ReSource processing facility in Lewiston, ME. Nevertheless, LD 1639 passed, and the ReSource facility remains open.
During the "Sludge Crisis" of 2023, Casella put Maine on the brink of a public health crisis by refusing to receive more sewage sludge unless the State allowed them to bring in 235,000 tons of out-of-state construction waste annually. The public and the Legislature pushed back, asking for proof that such a high volume was necessary. Casella ultimately revised its request to 25,000 tons a year, revealing their initial demand was profit-driven, not need-based.

Thanks to public and legislative resistance, Casella proceeded with the legally required stages of the expansion process without such a guarantee. Now, through LD 297, Casella is trying once again to undo the protections of LD 1639, and reopen JRL to out-of-state waste.

Casella's business model depends on burying as much waste as possible, incentivizing it to prioritize profit over the health of Mainers and the protection of our environment. Time and again, it has fallen to the public and the Legislature to defend Maine's natural resources and communities against these pressures.
